planting.note: Sow or set corms in fall into lean, sharply drained sand so winter cold can break corm dormancy, siting plants in full sun on an open, sandy slope that mimics longleaf pine sandhill habitat.

directions: This longleaf pine sandhill endemic of the southeastern coastal plain, from the southern Carolinas through the Florida Panhandle into southern Alabama, produces a slender, unbranched spike in which the disc-only flower heads line up along one side of the stem rather than spiraling evenly around it. The pale pinkish-white to whitish florets open in late summer into fall, later than many purple-flowered blazing stars, giving pollinators an additional nectar source as the season winds down. Like other sandhill specialists it grows from a corm and demands deep, loose, excessively drained sand; it struggles and rots quickly in garden loam or clay. Best used in open, sunny, sand-based native plantings or rock gardens rather than conventional perennial borders.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant corms or fall-sown seed into clay-loam or sandy-loam coastal prairie soil in full sun, firming soil well since the species' native coastal prairie habitat is largely undrained but not waterlogged.

directions: Native to the remaining coastal prairie fragments, roadsides, and railroad rights-of-way of south Texas, this corm-forming blazing star sends up a smooth, hairless stem bearing a loose, airy spike of purple-lavender, bottlebrush-like flower heads that sit farther apart than the densely packed spikes of garden Liatris spicata. It blooms later than most of its relatives, typically from late summer into October, making it a valuable late nectar source for migrating monarchs and native bees moving through the Gulf Coast corridor. Habitat loss from prairie conversion has made it a plant of conservation concern in Texas, so garden use doubles as a small contribution to ex-situ preservation of the species. Grow in full sun with reliable drainage and avoid soils that stay saturated through winter.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated corms into thin, rocky, dolomite-derived or otherwise alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun, replicating the open glade conditions this species needs to persist.

directions: Known in the wild only from the Ketona dolomite glades of Bibb County, Alabama, this is one of the most range-restricted blazing stars in cultivation, a critically imperiled species whose entire native population occupies a handful of thin-soiled outcrops. It stays noticeably shorter than most eastern Liatris and carries fewer flower heads per spike, true to its species name, and it blooms earlier in the season (around early summer) than the late-summer bloom typical of the genus. Because it is adapted to shallow, mineral-rich, calcareous soil with almost no organic buildup, it needs lean, extremely well-drained conditions and will rot in average garden soil. Only grow nursery-propagated stock, never wild-collected material, given the species' precarious conservation status.

planting.note: Site nursery-propagated corms on a well-drained slope with humus-rich but free-draining soil and filtered light, echoing the wooded ravine edges where this species naturally grows.

directions: This blazing star was only formally described in the early 2000s and is restricted to bluffs and ravines along the upper Apalachicola River in the Florida Panhandle, making it one of just two Liatris species confined to that region. Unlike most of its open-prairie relatives, it is found on shaded to partly shaded slope habitat with steadier soil moisture, so it tolerates more shade and a richer, moisture-retentive soil than sandhill or glade blazing stars. Its rose-purple flower spikes still follow the familiar late-summer blazing-star bloom pattern and draw bees and butterflies. Given its critically imperiled status in the wild, with seed held in conservation seed banks, gardeners should source only nursery-grown material and treat any planting as a conservation-minded addition to a woodland-edge native garden.
sources: Florida Plant Atlas (University of South Florida)
